verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “terrible headaches since midday on the left side…,” and confirms to doctor it “started at midday a few hours ago.” Headache described as throbbing: “Yeah, I guess it's throbbing on that left side.”

Same as cc-001: left-sided, throbbing (“it's throbbing on that left side”), sudden (“No, really, it just happened”), started at midday and has lasted a few hours (“started at midday a few hours ago”).

Patient says, “I noticed some zigzag lines in my vision. A few minutes before the headache started, my vision blurred… It feels like it's on both [eyes].” This supports visual aura with zig-zag lines and transient bilateral blurred vision before the headache.
Doctor asks about bright lights; patient replies, “Yeah, well, I'm wearing sunglasses right now. You know, light's really hurting my eyes.” This supports photophobia and wearing sunglasses.
Patient: “I just feel like I need to vomit.” Later, in response to doctor: “Yeah, I vomited twice.” This supports nausea and two vomiting episodes.
Patient: “No, but it's worse when I move… if I lean forward or like move my head or neck. Yeah, the headache gets worse.” This explicitly links worsening to head/neck movement.
Doctor: “Any temperatures or fevers?” Patient: “No, I don't feel feverish.” This is a denial of fever.
Doctor: “Any other funny skin rashes that you may have noticed?” Patient: “No, I haven't noticed anything like that.” This is a denial of rash.
Doctor: “Have you noticed any problems with your speech at all? Any difficulty with words?” Patient: “No.” This is a denial of speech difficulty.
Doctor: “Any problems with your arms and legs, for example, numbness or weakness?” Patient: “No.” This is a denial of focal weakness.
Doctor: “Any difficulty with balance, your balance or coordination?” Patient: “No.” This is a denial of balance issues.
Doctor: “Have you had any injuries to your head? Have you had a fall recently or been knocked on the head?” Patient: “No.” This denies head trauma.
Doctor: “you're feeling otherwise okay. So for example, your breathing is okay, you're not feeling breathless or. No.” The patient’s “No” indicates denial of breathlessness/shortness of breath.
Patient: “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago.” When asked duration: “For a couple of days.” This supports a similar episode a few weeks ago lasting about two days.

Patient: “I've just been googling and like I've read, you know, if your headache gets worse when you move, it could be a sign of brain cancer… Is that what you're worried about? … Oh, yeah, yeah.” This shows concern about brain tumour after online search.
Patient: “my friend's mum, she recently died of a brain tumor.” This exactly supports the statement.
Doctor: “Do you have any other medical history I should be aware of?” Patient: “No.” No other past medical conditions are reported in the transcript.
Patient: “I take the pill, microgynon.” Doctor: “And how long have you been on that for?” Patient: “Three months.” Confirms Microgynon OCP for three months.
Patient: “My mum had. Has migraines, but I've not been diagnosed.” This supports maternal history of migraines.
Patient: “My mum has an underactive thyroid as well.” Underactive thyroid is hypothyroidism.
Patient: “working fashion industry and you know, they're wondering what's going on.” Confirms work in fashion industry.

Doctor: “Is your job quite stressful at the moment?” Patient: “Yeah, it's really stressful, actually. Having problems with like people at work… managers like putting a lot of pressure on me…” This supports high job stress.
Doctor: “Who's at home with you?” Patient: “I live on my own.” Confirms living alone.
Doctor: “Do you smoke at all?” Patient: “No.” Confirms non-smoker.
Doctor: “And do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient: “No.” Confirms not drinking alcohol.
Doctor: “Do you do much in the way of exercise?” Patient: “No.” Supports lack of regular exercise.

Doctor mentions intent to examine but no examination or vitals are described: “normally at this I'd like to kind of proceed to examination, but based on your story…” So it is accurate that no physical findings or vital signs are recorded in the transcript.

Doctor: “I wonder whether you may. May have a migraine. Migraine type headache. It sounds very classical of that nature. The headache on one side, throbbing nature, the nausea, vomiting, sensitive to bright lights. I'm reassured that you don't have anything more serious, such as meningitis or indeed brain cancer.” There are recurrent episodes (current plus similar a few weeks ago) and no red-flag neurological signs as explicitly denied earlier.

Patient repeatedly expresses fear of brain cancer: “I've just been googling… sign of brain cancer… What if it is a brain tumor? What's going to happen with my future, my career?” This supports health anxiety about brain tumour.
Doctor: “Some strong painkillers would be advisable. So, you know, think about paracetamol or even cocodamol and some anti inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen.” Matches the plan content.
Doctor: “I think keeping a headache diary will be quite important to see exactly what's triggering these headaches.” This is explicit advice to keep a headache diary.

Doctor explains: “I wonder whether you may. May have a migraine… It sounds very classical… I'm reassured that you don't have anything more serious, such as meningitis or indeed brain cancer.” This educates about migraine and reassures low suspicion for intracranial mass/brain cancer.

Doctor: “if your symptoms aren't getting better in the next two, three days, or indeed they're getting worse… So if your headache's getting worse and not responding to medications, or your neck pain is getting worse, or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs or your vision, then I want you to come back…” This covers persistence 2–3 days, increasing headache, neurological deficits, visual changes, and worsening neck pain as reasons to return.

Doctor: “if your headaches were to become more persistent, then we can maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening in the first place. Something prophylactic medicines. Okay, we can have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps. … That's something we May have a little discussion about today as well [re: pill].” This implies follow-up next week with possible prophylactic treatment and discussion of the pill if attacks continue.
Doctor: “we can have a discussion next time I see you next week, perhaps.” This explicitly indicates a follow-up visit next week.
